name: Bayesian Linear Regression
analogy: Think of it as a forecaster who states a belief before looking at any data, such as most indicators probably do little, and then revises that belief bar by bar as evidence comes in. The answer is never one line but a bundle of plausible lines, so the forecast arrives with an honest margin of error that is wide when data is thin.

steps.title: State a prior belief about every weight
steps.description: Each feature gets a weight, and before seeing any data the model states what weights are plausible. The usual choice is a bell curve centered on zero, meaning most features probably matter very little. This acts as automatic protection against overfitting.
steps.inExample: Before seeing any bars, the weight on every feature, such as the past 6-bar return, is believed to be near zero, within a modest spread.

steps.title: Measure how well each possible weight fits the data
steps.description: The training bars are then used to score every possible set of weights by how likely the observed returns would be under it. Weights that explain the data well score high; weights that explain it badly score low.
steps.inExample: From the last 2,000 five-minute bars, weights that predict the next 30-minute return well score higher than weights that predict it badly.

steps.title: Combine belief and evidence into a posterior
steps.description: Belief and evidence are multiplied together to give a new, updated set of plausible weights called the posterior. With a bell-curve belief and bell-curve noise this is exact arithmetic, as cheap as ordinary regression. The posterior is narrow where the data is decisive and stays wide where it is not.
steps.inExample: The weight on the past 6-bar return settles slightly below zero with a wide range, while the weight on volume stays near zero.

steps.title: Add the noise the market always has
steps.description: Even with perfect weights, returns scatter around the line. The model estimates this noise from the data, so the final forecast range combines the market's own scatter with the leftover doubt about the weights.
steps.inExample: Bar-to-bar scatter of the 30-minute move is about 52 points, and the weight doubt adds a little, making the total spread 54 points.

steps.title: Forecast a whole bell curve for the new bar
steps.description: For a new bar the model passes its features through the plausible weights and returns a bell curve: a center, which is the expected move, and a spread, which is how unsure it is. A bar whose features look unlike the training data gets a wider curve.
steps.inExample: For the 10:20 bar the curve is centered on plus 8 points with a spread of 54 points.

steps.title: Keep updating as bars arrive
steps.description: After each new batch of bars, today's posterior becomes tomorrow's starting belief, so the model learns continuously without retraining on the whole history.
steps.inExample: After the next day's 78 bars, the weights are nudged and the forecast spread narrows very slightly.

useFor.task: Return forecasts that come with honest error bars
useFor.example: Forecasting the next 30-minute MNQ move as a center and a range, so a trade is only taken when the range leans clearly to one side.
Cutting position size from 4 contracts to 2 when the forecast range doubles because the training window was short or the market regime changed.

useFor.task: Learning continuously from a stream of bars
useFor.example: Updating the model after every 5-minute bar so it follows slow drift in how features relate to returns.

useFor.task: Finding which indicators the data really supports
useFor.example: Using the automatic-relevance variant to shrink most of the 151 technical indicators to zero and keep the handful the data supports.

avoidWhen: The relationship between features and target is strongly nonlinear; gradient boosting or a neural network can capture bends and interactions that a weighted sum cannot.
Returns are far from bell-shaped around a news release; heavy tails make the bell-curve forecast range too narrow for those bars.

example.scenario: At 10:20 on an MNQ 5-minute chart, a Bayesian linear model trained on the previous 2,000 bars is asked for a forecast of the move over the next 30 minutes, which is 6 bars.

input.summary: One row of features for the bar that just closed, plus the size of the training window.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 10:20 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: move over the last 6 bars
fields.meaning: How far price has fallen over the previous 30 minutes.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; lower values mean recent selling dominated.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, a measure of current movement.

fields.name: training window
fields.meaning: How many past bars the posterior weights were learned from.

output.summary: A bell curve for the next 30-minute move: where it is centered and how wide it is.

fields.name: expected move over the next 6 bars
fields.meaning: The center of the forecast curve.

fields.name: forecast spread
fields.meaning: One standard deviation of the curve, combining market scatter and weight doubt.

fields.name: 80 percent range
fields.meaning: The interval that should hold the true move about eight times in ten if the model is calibrated.

fields.name: chance the move is up
fields.meaning: The share of the forecast curve that lies above zero.

example.reading: The center is tiny next to the spread, so this is a very weak lean, not a signal. A trade needs the lean to cover costs: 8 points on one MNQ contract is 16 US dollars against a round-trip cost of about 2 US dollars, before any variation. Check on later bars that realized moves landed inside the 80 percent range about 80 percent of the time.
